newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary synagogue reopens, sign of Judaism revival.
newsitem.headline: Hungary synagogue reopens, sign of Judaism revival.

text.p: With the blare of a ram's horn to start the service, Jews from Hungary and around the world reopened Europe's biggest synagogue on Thursday, marking a revival of Judaism in the region.

More than 7,000 people, including Nazi labour camp survivors, former Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Shamir, Hungarian government officials, Christian clerics and thousands of Jews jammed into the newly restored synagogue in Budapest.

"It's wonderful. This happens only once in a person's lifetime," said labour camp survivor Kalman Veszi, 72, with tears streaming down his cheeks as he stood in the pews of the Dohanyi Utca synagogue for the two and a half hour service.
"Something unexpected, extraordinary has happened...this is a moment that cannot be repeated," he said.
Former Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Shamir, whose family was wiped out in Nazi camps during World War Two, brought a message for the Hungarian people from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"I feel honoured to convey the best wishes of the Israeli prime minister and government for the reopening of this grand building," Shamir, whose remarks were translated from Hebrew by Israel's ambassador to Hungary, Joel Alon, said.

"We remember our brothers who carried the burden and endured the suffering of the Jewish people and were brave enough to face the evil that killed several hundred thousand (Hungarian) Jews," Shamir said.
"At the same time we feel happy because those who hate us have not managed to destroy us."
The 137-year-old synagogue, the largest outside the U.S. and as long as a soccer field, was extensively damaged during World War Two.

The building was hit by 27 bombs and served as shelter for thousands of Jews after the Nazi-aligned government created a Jewish ghetto in Budapest. Hungary had a population of 800,000 Jews before the war but 600,000 died in camps under the Nazis.
There are 80,000 to 100,000 Jews in Hungary today.

The elegant, gold-domed, Moorish-style temple has been rebuilt at a cost of 1.35 billion forints ($9 million), 80 percent of which was donated by the Hungarian government. The rest came from the international Jewish community.
Hungarian President Arpad Goncz, who sat in the front row beside Shamir, said World War Two had been a "murderous period" in Hungary when tens of thousands of people were killed.
"The Jewish community in Hungary today is again capable to create and to integrate with the entire people of Hungary."

After the blowing of the "shofar" horn, young women walked up the mosaiced aisles, strewing flower petals for a procession of members of the Hungarian Jewish community carrying the Torah, or Jewish holy scrolls.
The men placed the scrolls inside the synagogue's 8.2-metre (26-foot) tall Ark of the Covenant, a gilded cupboard, signifying that God had returned to the temple.
The scrolls had been removed for safekeeping while the synagogue remained in a state of near-collapse under the communist authorities who ruled Hungary until 1989.
Also attending was U.S. congressman Tom Lantos, a Hungarian native who celebrated his barmitzvah, the Jewish coming of age rite, in the synagogue before World War Two.

Lantos, who escaped Hungary with the help of Swedish diplomat Raoul Wallenberg, who aided thousands of Jews before he was arrested by the Soviets and disappeared in prison, said before the ceremony that the world must fight anti-Semitism, including incidents of Jewish cemetery vandalism in Hungary.
"The veneer of civilisation is paper-thin and it is our job both in the public and the private sectors to make that veneer a bit more durable and strong," Lantos told Reuters.
